narration: Here's something strange. One of these funds charges you almost nothing. Another charges two percent a year plus twenty percent of your profits — and, as a group, still loses to the cheap one. Yet they often own nearly the same things.
caption: what they charge you

narration: A top hedge fund can take fifty times more in fees than a simple index fund — for results that, over time, are usually worse. So why does anyone pick the expensive one?
Mutual funds, index funds, ETFs, hedge funds — the names get thrown around like they're wildly different beasts. In truth, three of them are cousins, and one is the odd, exclusive one out.

memeBottom: three are the same idea in different wrappers
narration: So let's untangle all four — because understanding the difference is worth, quite literally, a fortune in fees over your lifetime.
Start with the one idea they all share.
heading: One Shared Idea

narration: Every one of these is a 'fund' — a way to pool your money with thousands of other people, so that together you can buy a huge basket of assets no single one of you could afford alone.
That's the magic of a fund. A little money from a lot of people becomes one giant pot — instantly spreading your risk across dozens, hundreds, even thousands of different investments.
caption: many wallets → one big pool

narration: The idea is a century old. The first modern mutual fund appeared in the 1920s, letting ordinary people pool their savings and own a slice of the whole market for the very first time. It democratized investing.
The differences come down to just four questions. Who runs it? How do you buy it? What does it cost? And who's even allowed in? Answer those, and you've mastered all four types.
First, the original: the mutual fund.
heading: The Mutual Fund

narration: A mutual fund is an investment fund that pools money from many investors to purchase securities. It's the grandparent of the whole family.

One classic trap with older mutual funds is the 'load' — a sales commission, sometimes five percent, skimmed off the top the moment you buy in. Always look for 'no-load' funds, where every dollar you invest actually gets invested.

A professional manager runs it, deciding what to buy and sell. You hand over your money, they invest it, and you own a slice of the whole pot. Simple, and for decades, the default way ordinary people invested.

But the classic mutual fund has two quirks. One: it's usually 'actively managed,' so it charges higher fees for that manager's supposed skill. Two: you can only buy or sell it once a day, at a single set price.

There's also a quieter mechanical split: most funds are 'open-end,' creating new shares as money flows in. A few are 'closed-end,' with a fixed number of shares that trade at their own price — a detail that trips up a lot of beginners.
Which brings us to its cheaper, smarter child: the index fund.
heading: The Index Fund

narration: Here's the key confusion to clear up. An index fund isn't really a separate competitor. It's a style of fund — one that can be packaged as either a mutual fund or an ETF. The difference is what's inside.
An index fund simply aims to replicate a market index by holding the same securities as the index — instead of a manager trying to pick winners.

label: JOHN BOGLE
caption: invented the index fund
narration: This is the invention of John Bogle: don't pay a manager to guess. Just buy the whole market, keep fees microscopic, and quietly beat most of the pros who are trying so hard.
Because it just copies a list instead of paying a star manager, the index fund is astonishingly cheap — often charging a few cents per hundred dollars, versus a dollar or more for active funds.
caption: small fees, enormous gap

title: The fund family tree
narration: Here's the family tree in time. The first mutual fund in the 1920s. Bogle's first index fund in 1976, mocked at launch. The first ETF in 1993. And by 2019, passive funds overtaking active ones entirely.

That passive revolution is staggering in scale. Firms like Vanguard and BlackRock now manage tens of trillions of dollars in cheap index funds and ETFs — a tidal wave of money that fled the expensive, actively-managed world.
Now the modern superstar, the one that trades like a stock: the ETF.
heading: The ETF

narration: An exchange-traded fund, or ETF, is an investment fund that is bought and sold on stock exchanges — trading all day long, just like a share of a company.

That's the crucial difference from a mutual fund. A mutual fund prices once a day, after the market closes. An ETF has a live, moving price all day, and you can buy or sell it in a single click, any time.
caption: same idea, different plumbing

narration: ETFs have a sneaky tax advantage, too. Thanks to a clever share-creation mechanism, they rarely pass taxable gains onto you while you hold them — so, outside a retirement account especially, they can quietly beat an identical mutual fund.
Most ETFs are actually index funds in a sleeker wrapper — cheap, tracking an index, but tradeable live. They're also usually more tax-efficient, which is why they've quietly exploded in popularity.

title: Fee over 30 years on $100k ($ lost)
narration: Put the fees in real money. On a hundred thousand dollars over thirty years, a rock-bottom index fee costs you a few thousand. A one-percent active fee costs tens of thousands. The hedge-fund model can cost a fortune.
For most people, the choice between an index mutual fund and an index ETF barely matters. They can hold the exact same thing. One just trades live, and the other prices once a day.
It is the great running joke of modern finance: paying the highest fees in the industry, very often, buys you the privilege of below-average returns.
And finally, the exclusive, expensive, mysterious one: the hedge fund.
heading: The Hedge Fund

narration: A hedge fund is a pooled investment fund that makes use of complex trading and risk-management techniques — far beyond simply buying and holding stocks.

Hedge funds can do things normal funds can't: short-selling to profit when prices fall, piling on leverage, and making huge bets on currencies, commodities, or whole economies. High risk, in search of high reward.

Hedge funds come in many flavors. 'Long-short' funds bet on some stocks rising and others falling. 'Global macro' funds, like Soros's, bet on whole economies. 'Quant' funds, like Simons's, let the algorithms decide. Each a different way to gamble for an edge.
But the first thing to know is that you probably can't even invest in one. Hedge funds are gated — legally restricted to the wealthy and big institutions, not the general public.
caption: one of them has a velvet rope

narration: That's because they're marketed only to institutional investors and high-net-worth individuals — the exclusive club of big money.

And the exclusivity comes with a catch: your money can get locked up. Many hedge funds impose 'lock-up' periods, where you simply cannot withdraw your cash for months or years. An index ETF, by contrast, you can sell in seconds.

label: RAY DALIO
caption: built the biggest hedge fund
narration: The legends are real. Ray Dalio built Bridgewater into the biggest hedge fund on Earth, managing the money of pensions and governments with his own grand theories of how economies work.

label: JIM SIMONS
caption: the quant who truly beat the market
narration: And Jim Simons, a mathematician, built Renaissance — whose secretive quant fund posted returns so absurdly good they may be the best in all of financial history. These outliers are why the dream persists.

Be very skeptical of the dazzling hedge-fund track records, too. Thousands of funds launch; the losers quietly shut down and vanish from the averages. What you see is survivorship bias — the flattering, cherry-picked survivors.
But those legends hide the thing that really defines a hedge fund: the fees.
heading: The Fees

narration: Hedge funds famously charge what's called 'two and twenty.' That means two percent of all your money every year, no matter what — plus twenty percent of any profits they make.
Think about how brutal that is. Even in a flat year where they make you nothing, they take two percent. And when they do win, they pocket a fifth of your profit before you see a cent.
caption: 2% of everything + 20% of profits

narration: The most famous proof is Warren Buffett's bet. He wagered a million dollars that a simple index fund would beat a basket of elite hedge funds over ten years. He won in a landslide, and gave the winnings to charity.
It all comes down to the expense ratio — the annual cost of owning a fund. And across these four, that single number varies more than almost anything else.

And here's the punchline the industry hates. After those enormous fees, the average hedge fund has, for many years, failed to beat a simple, cheap index fund that a child could buy. You pay a fortune to underperform.

memeBottom: still trailing a free index fund
narration: For most hedge-fund clients, that's the quiet reality underneath the glamour: enormous fees, lock-ups, and complexity, in exchange for returns a cheap fund would have beaten.

memeBottom: for most people, a cheap index ETF beats an expensive hedge fund
narration: For the tiny handful of true geniuses like Simons, the fees are worth it. For the vast majority of hedge funds, you're paying Ferrari prices for a car that finishes behind the bus.

So why do they still exist? Partly the dream of the next Simons. Partly because the ultra-rich want something exclusive, uncorrelated, or tailored. And partly, frankly, because 'I'm in a hedge fund' sounds a lot better at dinner than 'I own an index fund.'
So let's line all four up, side by side.
heading: The Showdown

narration: Index funds: cheap, passive, own-everything. Mutual funds: often active, priced daily. ETFs: cheap and tradeable live. Hedge funds: pricey, exclusive, complex. Four wrappers around the same core idea.
caption: four ways to own a basket of assets

narration: Compare the two honest paths for a normal person. Pick your own stocks, and you're a lone amateur against the pros. Buy one index fund, and you instantly own a slice of everything, cheaply.

Three of them — index funds, most ETFs, and passive mutual funds — are really the same sensible strategy: own the whole market cheaply. The hedge fund is the one playing a completely different, far riskier game.

There are handy hybrids, too. A 'target-date fund' automatically shifts you from risky stocks toward safer bonds as you age — a whole retirement strategy, on autopilot, inside a single fund you never have to touch.
Which leaves the only question that matters: which one is for you?
heading: Who Wins

narration: The data, again, is blunt. Over the long run, the cheap, boring, passive options reliably beat the expensive, exciting, active ones. Cost is the single best predictor of who wins.
caption: who actually wins, long-term

narration: So for almost everyone, the answer is a low-cost index fund or index ETF. It's cheap, it's diversified, it requires no genius, and it quietly outperforms the fancy stuff over time.

memeBottom: go wrong with a low-cost, broad index fund
narration: It is genuinely hard to make a serious mistake with a cheap, diversified index fund held for the long term. That's exactly what makes it such a powerful default.

Buying one is now trivial. Open a brokerage account, search for a broad, low-cost index fund or ETF, and buy it like any stock. The whole thing can take about ten minutes — the hard part, as always, is just leaving it alone.

An actively-managed mutual fund can make sense in a few niche corners. And a hedge fund can make sense if you're ultra-wealthy, chasing a specific edge, and fully understand the odds. For everyone else? Keep it simple.
So let's total up the four funds.
heading: The Final Math

narration: A mutual fund pools money, priced daily. An index fund just tracks the market, cheaply. An ETF does that but trades live. A hedge fund charges a fortune to gamble — for the wealthy only.
lines: index fund → tracks the market, cheap
ETF → like an index fund, trades live

narration: Strip away the jargon and it's almost funny how simple it is. They are all just baskets. The real differences are cost, how you buy, and who's allowed in — and on cost, cheaper has reliably meant richer.

Step back and the shift is historic. Trillions of dollars have marched out of expensive, hand-picked funds and into cheap, automatic ones — the biggest quiet victory for ordinary investors in a generation.

props.label: a win for the little guy

narration: So the next time someone brags about their exclusive hedge fund, you can smile — and remember that the boring index ETF in your pocket has quietly beaten most of them, for a fraction of the price.
